1rjb9o5.t:
Good morning. Today I want to talk about something every student cares about, which is how to remember what you study. Let's start with a common habit. Many students prepare for exams by rereading their notes and highlighting key sentences. It feels productive. The text looks familiar, and familiarity gives us a sense that we know the material. Unfortunately, research consistently shows that rereading is one of the least effective study methods. Recognising information is not the same as being able to recall it.

So what works better? The first strategy is called retrieval practice. Instead of looking at the information again, you try to bring it back from memory. This could mean answering practice questions, using flashcards, or simply closing your book and writing down everything you can remember about a topic. In one well-known experiment, students who read a passage once and then tested themselves remembered around fifty per cent more a week later than students who read it several times. The effort of retrieving is exactly what strengthens the memory.

The second strategy is spacing. When we cram, we pack all our study into one long session just before the exam. Cramming can work for the next day, but the information fades quickly. If, instead, you spread your study over several shorter sessions, separated by days, you remember much more over the long term. A useful rule of thumb is to review new material the next day, then a few days later, then a week later.

The third strategy is interleaving, which means mixing different types of problems rather than practising one type at a time. In mathematics, for example, students often complete twenty questions on the same skill. Interleaving mixes questions from different topics. It feels harder, and students usually believe they are learning less. But because they must decide which method to use each time, their performance in tests is often significantly better.

Now, you might be wondering why so many people still rely on rereading and cramming. The answer is that effective learning often feels difficult, while ineffective learning feels easy. Researchers call these desirable difficulties. My advice is to trust the evidence rather than your feelings. If studying feels slightly uncomfortable, that may be a sign that it is working.

For next week, I'd like you to try one of these strategies in another subject and keep a short record of what you did. We'll compare notes in the tutorial.

2lgmdf.t: Thanks for coming in. I wanted to talk about your essay on assessment practices.
Sure. I was a bit disappointed with my mark.
I understand. Your ideas are strong, and your examples from your placement were excellent. The main issue was structure. Your argument wasn't clear until the final page.
So I should state my position earlier?
Exactly, in the introduction. Then each paragraph should begin with a topic sentence linking back to that position.
Mostly good, but several sources were more than ten years old. The task asked for recent research, ideally from the last five years.
It's in the marking rubric. I'd recommend checking the rubric before you start and again before you submit. For the next assignment, you're welcome to send me an outline a week before the deadline.

19mogu1.t:
Welcome back to the show. Today I want to talk about habits, and why some are so easy to form while others seem impossible. Researchers estimate that a large part of what we do each day is habitual. We don't consciously decide to brush our teeth or check our phones; we simply do it.

A habit is usually described as a loop with three parts. First, there's a cue, something that triggers the behaviour, like waking up or feeling bored. Second, there's the routine, which is the behaviour itself. And third, there's a reward, the good feeling that makes the brain want to repeat it. Checking your phone, for example, can be triggered by boredom and rewarded by a small hit of novelty.

So how long does it take to form a new habit? You may have heard twenty-one days. In fact, one well-known study from University College London found it took participants an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic, with a huge range from about eighteen days to over two hundred, depending on the person and the habit. Simple habits, like drinking a glass of water at breakfast, formed faster than complex ones, like doing fifty sit-ups before dinner.

The good news is that missing a day didn't seriously damage progress. What mattered was consistency over time.

So what does this mean in practice? Experts suggest three strategies. Start very small. If you want to exercise, begin with five minutes, not an hour. Link the new habit to an existing one, a technique called habit stacking. For instance, after I pour my morning coffee, I'll write one sentence in my journal. And change your environment. If you want to eat more fruit, put it on the bench; if you want to use your phone less, leave it in another room.

Breaking bad habits works in reverse. Make the cue harder to notice and the behaviour harder to do. Willpower, it turns out, is far less reliable than design.

rq84py.t: Today we're discussing whether the school day should change. With me is education researcher Professor Leanne Moore. Leanne, most Australian schools run from about nine until three. Where did that come from?
Largely from history. The timetable developed when many families had one parent at home and children were needed for chores. Society has changed a great deal, but the school day mostly hasn't.
Some people argue high schools should start later. Why?

Sleep research shows that teenagers' body clocks shift, so they naturally fall asleep and wake later. When schools start early, many students are chronically tired. Studies from the United States found that when some high schools moved their start time to around eight-thirty or later, attendance improved, students reported better mood, and there were fewer car accidents involving teenage drivers.
So why don't all schools do it?

Practical reasons. Later starts affect bus timetables, which are often shared with primary schools. They push after-school sport and part-time jobs later. And many parents rely on schools for childcare while they work.
Are there other ideas for changing the day?

Yes. Some schools are trialling flexible timetables, where senior students attend fewer days on campus and study independently on others. Others offer extended hours with optional before- and after-school programs, which helps working parents. In some countries, schools have longer breaks in the middle of the day.

I don't think there's one perfect model. But I'd like to see more schools trial later starts for older students and measure the results carefully. Decisions should be based on evidence and on consultation with students, families and teachers, rather than on habit.

1rfpr3c.t:
Hi everyone. With the HSC only a few months away, I want to talk about stress, because nearly everyone in this room will feel some.

First, a little stress is actually useful. It increases focus and motivation; it's what gets you to open the textbook. Problems begin when stress becomes constant and overwhelming. Signs include trouble sleeping, headaches, irritability, feeling unable to concentrate, or withdrawing from friends. If you notice these, it's time to act.

So what helps? Let me give you four things. Number one: plan, don't panic. Break your revision into specific tasks, like complete two past papers for chemistry, rather than vague goals like study chemistry. Use a calendar and work backwards from your exam dates. A plan reduces the feeling that everything needs to be done at once.

Number two: protect your sleep. It's tempting to stay up late, but memory is consolidated while you sleep. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam usually lowers your performance.

Number three: keep moving and keep connected. Even a twenty-minute walk reduces stress hormones. Don't drop your sport or your part-time job completely, and spend time with friends. Balance is not a distraction from study; it makes study possible.

Number four: watch your self-talk. Thoughts like I'm going to fail everything or my life is over if I don't get my ATAR are common, but they're not facts. Try replacing them with something more realistic, like I've prepared for this and I'll do my best. Remember too that there are many pathways to university and careers, including bridging courses, TAFE and early entry programs.

Finally, ask for help. Your teachers, year adviser and school counsellor are here for you. Services like Kids Helpline and headspace are available too.

You've got this. And whatever happens, your results don't define your worth.

1ui5fc0.t:
Thank you for coming to tonight's talk. I'd like to start with a question: how many of you have ever counted birds in your backyard, photographed a frog, or reported a whale sighting? If you have, you may already be a citizen scientist.

Citizen science means members of the public taking part in real scientific research, usually by collecting or analysing data. It isn't new; amateur naturalists have contributed to science for centuries. But smartphones and the internet have transformed what's possible. Today, one person's photo, uploaded to an app with a time and location, can become part of a data set used by researchers around the world.

Let me give you some Australian examples. The FrogID project asks people to record frog calls on their phones. Each species has a distinctive call, so experts can identify which frogs are present. Volunteers have submitted hundreds of thousands of recordings, helping scientists track how frogs responded to bushfires and drought, and even contributing to the discovery of species in new locations.

The Aussie Bird Count runs every October and involves people counting birds for twenty minutes. And projects like Redmap ask fishers and divers to report marine species seen outside their usual range, which helps scientists understand how warming oceans are shifting where species live.

Why does this matter? Professional scientists simply can't be everywhere. Citizen scientists provide data across huge areas and long periods of time, at very low cost. Participants also benefit. Research shows they gain scientific knowledge, feel more connected to nature and often become advocates for conservation.

Of course, there are challenges. Data quality can vary, so projects use expert checking and verification tools. Most participants also come from cities and from groups with higher education, so researchers are working to include more diverse communities, including Aboriginal rangers who bring deep knowledge of Country.

So tonight, I encourage you to download one of these apps and become part of the research.

159kddd.t:
Good morning, everyone. I'd like to begin with a confession. In my first year of teaching, I planned what I thought was a brilliant lesson on probability, with dice, cards and a class competition. Within ten minutes, the room was chaos, two students were arguing, and nobody had learned anything about probability. I went home convinced I had chosen the wrong career.

I tell this story because we rarely talk honestly about failure in education, even though it's one of the most powerful sources of learning, for teachers and for students.

Research on what's often called productive failure supports this. In a series of studies, students who first attempted challenging problems on their own, and mostly failed, before receiving instruction, later showed deeper understanding than students who were taught the method first. The struggle seemed to prepare their minds to make sense of the explanation. The key word, though, is productive. The problems must be within reach, students must feel safe to make mistakes, and the teacher must then help them connect their attempts to the correct ideas.

That sense of safety matters enormously. If students believe mistakes will be punished or mocked, they'll avoid challenges altogether. So how do we create a classroom where failure is acceptable? A few practical ideas. Talk about your own mistakes, as I just have. When a student gets something wrong, ask them to explain their thinking before correcting them; often the error reveals a reasonable idea. Give feedback that focuses on the next step rather than just a mark. And, where possible, allow students to revise and resubmit work.

The same applies to us as teachers. That disastrous probability lesson taught me to give clearer instructions, set roles in group work and test activities before using them. The second time I taught it, it worked well.

So my challenge for today is this: in your groups, share one lesson that didn't go as planned, and what you learned from it. Let's model the culture we want our students to experience.

Great. What did you have in mind?

I like that. We usually just draw one bar graph and move on. When would it run?

That works. Should we have one shared assessment?
I think so. A short report where students explain whether their data supports their hypothesis. We could mark it together using one rubric.
Good idea, but we'll need to moderate a few samples so our marking's consistent.

I'd suggest she comes to the Tuesday lunchtime help session. I'll also give her a short set of review questions each week, and I'll check in with her during class.

I think the start was good, but I ran out of time for practice.
I agree. Your explanation of gradient was very clear, and I liked the real example with the skateboard ramp.
Thanks. But I spent too long on the introduction.
Yes, about twenty minutes. Try to keep the explanation under ten, and then let them practise.
How do I know if they're ready to practise?
Use a quick check, like two questions on mini whiteboards. If most get it right, move on. If not, reteach with one more example.
That makes sense. What about the students at the back?
A few were off task. Walk around more during practice, and call on students by name.

I trialled MathsPath this term. Students liked the instant feedback, and completion went up a lot.

The reports are the main advantage of MathsPath. I can see which questions the whole class got wrong.
What about students without internet at home?

m1ry0i.t: Hi Leo, have you chosen a topic for your IPT major project?
I want to build a booking system for my dad's barber shop.
That's a great real-world problem. What does the system need to do?
Customers should book online, and my dad should see all the bookings for the day.
Good. So you'll need a database. What tables would you have?
Exactly. And how will you make sure two people can't book the same time?
Hmm, I hadn't thought about that.
That's called validation. Add it to your requirements. Also, think about privacy, because you'll store phone numbers.
Okay. Should I start coding now?
Not yet. First interview your dad about how bookings work now, then draw your data flow diagram. Show me next lesson.

eiziv2.t: Schools across New South Wales are updating their policies on artificial intelligence. At one high school in Western Sydney, the new policy allows students to use AI chatbots for brainstorming and checking their understanding, as long as they record how they used them in a short log. However, any work submitted for assessment must be the student's own. The head of computing, Mr Rahman, says the aim is to teach responsible use rather than ban the technology. In maths, teachers have introduced short oral checks, where students explain one question from their assignment. Mr Rahman says the checks take only two minutes per student but make it very clear whether students understand their work. Parents have generally been supportive, although some worry that students who don't have AI tools at home may be at a disadvantage.

atrucn.t: How was the PD day on differentiation?
Really useful, actually. The presenter showed how to plan one task with three entry points.
What does that look like in maths?
For example, with area, everyone works on the same problem, designing a garden. Some students get a grid and hints, most get the standard task, and others have a budget limit to make it harder.
So you're not writing three separate lessons?
Exactly. That's what I liked. It saves time and nobody feels singled out.
Yes. They suggested a short pre-test, so you can decide who needs which version.
I might try that with Year 9 next week.
I can share the slides with you.

zgedjn.t: A Sydney high school has reported strong results from a numeracy intervention program for Year 7 students. Teachers identified students who were more than two years behind in number skills using a diagnostic test at the start of the year. These students then attended small-group lessons three times a week, focusing on place value, fractions and multiplication. The lessons were run by trained learning support officers using a structured program. After two terms, most students had improved by at least one year's level, and many reported feeling more confident in their normal maths classes. The head teacher of mathematics says the key was early identification and consistency. However, she warns that the program depends on funding for support staff, which is not guaranteed for next year.

Hi, I'm a teacher at Granville High School. I'm hoping to book a speaker for our Maths Week.

18rvmx2.t: I've got a new student in Year 9 maths, Farid. He arrived from Afghanistan two months ago.
His maths is actually strong. He can solve equations quickly. But he struggles with word problems.
That's really common. The language is the barrier, not the maths.
Pre-teach the key vocabulary for each topic, words like 'total', 'difference', 'per'. A small glossary with pictures helps.
Let him work with a supportive partner, and if possible a student who speaks Dari.
There is one boy in the class who does.
Great. And talk to the EAL/D teacher; she can support you in class once a week.

18oogef.t:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to introduce cognitive load theory, which has become one of the most influential ideas in education research and is now referred to in many teacher training programs.

The theory is based on a simple observation about human memory. Our working memory, the part of the mind that holds information while we think, is very limited. Most adults can hold only a few new pieces of information at once. Long-term memory, on the other hand, is almost unlimited. Learning, in this view, is the process of building organised knowledge in long-term memory, sometimes called schemas.

Why does this matter for teachers? When students face too much new information at once, their working memory becomes overloaded, and very little is learned. This is particularly true for novices. An expert mathematician can solve a complex equation easily because many steps are automatic, stored in long-term memory. A Year 8 student must consciously process every step.

So what can we do? First, break complex material into smaller steps and teach them in a logical sequence. Second, use worked examples. Research shows that for beginners, studying a fully worked example is often more effective than solving the same problem independently. Then we can gradually remove steps, a technique called fading. Third, reduce unnecessary distractions. If a slide has an explanation in text and the teacher is also explaining it aloud, students may waste effort trying to read and listen at the same time. Diagrams should be placed next to the relevant text, not on a different page.

An important point is that as students become more expert, the support should change. Worked examples that help beginners can actually become less useful for advanced students, who benefit more from solving problems themselves. This is known as the expertise reversal effect.

For your planning this week, I'd like you to take one lesson and identify where students might be overloaded, then redesign it using worked examples and fading. We'll share these at our next meeting.

1tqt4cg.t: Today I'm speaking with Dr Helen Park, who researches computing education. Helen, how has computing in schools changed in the past decade?

Enormously. Ten years ago, computing was mainly an elective for students who were already interested in technology. Now, digital technologies are part of the curriculum from primary school, and students learn basic programming concepts much earlier.

It has increased awareness, but there's a big gap between what the curriculum says and what happens in classrooms. Many primary teachers, and even some secondary teachers, haven't had training in computing, so they lack confidence.
What about the senior years? In New South Wales, older courses like IPT and Software Design are being replaced.

That's right. Newer courses such as Software Engineering and Enterprise Computing focus more on current practices, like secure software development, data, and working with real clients. I think that's positive, because it connects school learning to industry.
What about artificial intelligence? Some people ask whether students still need to learn to code if AI can write code.

I hear that a lot. My answer is yes, but the focus is shifting. Students still need to understand how programs work so they can read, test and improve code, including code produced by AI. In fact, judging whether AI-generated code is correct and secure requires more understanding, not less.

Three things. First, teacher training, because quality teaching is the biggest factor. Second, equity. Students in regional areas and low-income communities often have less access to devices and specialist teachers. And third, ethics. Students should think about the impact of the technology they create, from privacy to bias.

1khp1dl.t:
Good morning, everyone. I'd like to talk about something every maths teacher struggles with at some point: engagement. How do we make students genuinely want to think about mathematics?

Let me start with a common misunderstanding. Engagement is not the same as entertainment. A lesson full of games and videos can be fun but produce very little learning. Real engagement happens when students are thinking hard about the mathematics itself.

So how do we achieve that? The first strategy is to start with a question rather than an answer. Instead of saying, "Today we're learning about the area of a circle," try showing a large pizza and a small pizza with their prices and asking, "Which is better value?" Students immediately want to know, and they need the mathematics to find out.

The second strategy is to use what's called low floor, high ceiling tasks. These are problems that every student can start, but that can be extended a long way. For example, "How many squares are there on a chessboard?" Every student can count the small squares, but the full answer requires systematic thinking, and the most able students can generalise to any size board.

Third, make students' thinking visible. Ask them to explain, compare strategies and critique each other's reasoning. When a student says, "I did it a different way," that's a golden moment for discussion.

Finally, success matters. Students who constantly fail switch off, so make sure tasks are challenging but achievable, and give students regular evidence of their progress. A short review quiz at the start of each lesson, where most students do well, can build confidence and remind them how much they've learned.

None of these strategies requires expensive resources. They require careful planning and a belief that every student can think mathematically. I'll now share some examples from my own classroom.

1kvl9d1.t:
Thank you for joining us tonight. My topic is digital wellbeing: how the technology young people use every day affects their health, relationships and learning.

First, some context. Most Australian teenagers now own a smartphone, and many spend several hours a day on screens outside school. Not all of this time is harmful. Teenagers use technology to stay in touch with friends, learn new skills and express their creativity. In fact, research suggests that moderate use is not associated with poorer wellbeing.

The concerns arise with heavy use, particularly late at night. Studies consistently link phone use in bed with shorter and poorer quality sleep, and lack of sleep affects mood, concentration and learning. Social media can also increase anxiety for some young people, especially when they compare themselves with idealised images or experience online conflict.

What can schools do? Many schools now restrict phone use during the day, and early reports suggest calmer classrooms and more face-to-face interaction. But restrictions alone are not enough. Students need to learn skills: how to manage notifications, recognise when an app is designed to keep them scrolling, protect their privacy and respond to online conflict. These skills can be taught in subjects like computing and personal development.

Parents also play a crucial role. One of the simplest and most effective steps is to keep devices out of bedrooms overnight, ideally charging them in a shared space. Parents can also model healthy habits, as children notice when adults are constantly on their phones.

Finally, it's important to involve young people in these conversations. When students help create family or school technology agreements, they are much more likely to follow them. Digital wellbeing is not about fear of technology; it's about helping young people use it in ways that support their lives rather than control them.

12nh6fd.t: Welcome to today's workshop. We'll be looking at how schools can use data to improve teaching. I'm joined by Sarah, a head teacher of mathematics. Sarah, how does your faculty use data?

We collect several types. There's external data like NAPLAN, but the most useful data comes from our own classrooms: short diagnostic tests, exit tickets and common assessments that all classes complete.
Because they let us compare. If one class does much better on a topic, we ask that teacher what they did differently. It's not about judging teachers; it's about sharing what works.

Last year our Year 8 results on ratios were weak across most classes, except one. That teacher had used a visual model called a bar model. We all tried it, and the next year the results improved significantly.
What are the risks of using data?

The biggest risk is collecting data and doing nothing with it. Another is focusing only on numbers. A test score doesn't tell you why a student is struggling. You still need to talk to students and look at their working.
How do you find the time?
We dedicate the first twenty minutes of every faculty meeting to looking at student work and data together. It's become a habit, and it's probably the most valuable twenty minutes of our week.
What advice would you give other schools?
Start small. Choose one year group and one topic, agree on a short common assessment, and meet to discuss the results. Make it about learning, not blame.

1hb76hh.t:
Good morning. Today we're focusing on probability, a topic that students often find counter-intuitive. Even adults make predictable errors. For example, many people believe that after five heads in a row, tails is now "due". This is known as the gambler's fallacy, and it shows how our intuition about chance can mislead us.

One of the most effective ways to build understanding is through simulation. Let's take a simple experiment: rolling two dice and adding the numbers. If you ask Year 9 students which total is most likely, many will guess that every total is equally likely. If they roll the dice twenty times, the results are too few to show a clear pattern. But if they use a spreadsheet or a short program to simulate ten thousand rolls, the pattern appears immediately: seven is the most common total, and two and twelve are the least.

This leads naturally to the idea of theoretical probability. Students can list all thirty-six possible outcomes in a table and discover that there are six ways to make seven, but only one way to make two. The simulation and the theory confirm each other, which is very powerful.

Simulations are also useful for introducing the law of large numbers: as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability. Students can see this happen by graphing results after ten, one hundred and ten thousand trials.

A practical tip: don't start with the technology. Let students roll real dice first and make predictions. When their small sample gives surprising results, they will want to know what happens with more trials, and that's the moment to introduce the simulation.

Finally, connect probability to real contexts, such as weather forecasts, sports statistics or games of chance. Discussing why casinos always make money over time can be a very memorable way to explore expected value with senior students.

13si8k1.t:
Hello, everyone. Behaviour management is consistently the area that beginning teachers worry about most, so let's look at what the research and experienced teachers say actually works.

The most important idea is that good behaviour is mostly built through prevention, not reaction. Teachers who rarely have serious problems are usually those who have taught clear routines from the first day. Students know exactly how to enter the room, how to start work, how to get help and how to pack up. When routines are clear, there are fewer opportunities for disruption.

Second, relationships matter. Learning students' names quickly, greeting them at the door and showing interest in their lives builds trust. Students are much more likely to cooperate with a teacher who they believe respects them.

Third, when problems occur, respond calmly and consistently. Use the least intrusive response first. Often a look, moving closer to the student or a quiet word is enough. Avoid public arguments, because students may feel they need to save face in front of their peers. If behaviour continues, follow the school's procedures and apply consequences consistently, so that students see the rules are fair.

Fourth, well-planned lessons prevent many problems. When work is too easy or too hard, students disengage. Having the first task ready as students enter and keeping transitions short reduces downtime, which is when most misbehaviour happens.

Finally, don't try to manage everything alone. Talk to your mentor, your head teacher and the year adviser. Experienced colleagues often know the students' backgrounds and can suggest strategies that work for particular individuals. Asking for help is a sign of professionalism, not weakness.

Remember that every experienced teacher had difficult lessons when they started. Reflect, adjust and keep going. Confidence will come.

lyoqnw.t:
Good afternoon. In today's lecture on software engineering, we're stepping away from code to discuss something just as important: ethics.

Software now makes decisions that affect people's lives. Algorithms help decide who gets a loan, which job applicants are interviewed and what news people see. When these systems are poorly designed, the consequences can be serious.

Let's consider three key issues. The first is bias. If a system is trained on historical data that reflects past discrimination, it may repeat that discrimination. For example, a recruitment tool trained on data from a company that mostly hired men might rank female applicants lower, even if no one intended this. Developers must test their systems for unfair outcomes across different groups.

The second issue is privacy. Many apps collect far more personal data than they need. The principle of data minimisation says that we should collect only what is necessary for the purpose. Developers should also consider how data is stored, who can access it and how long it is kept.

The third issue is accessibility. Software that cannot be used by people with disabilities excludes a significant part of the population. Simple practices, such as providing text descriptions for images, ensuring sufficient colour contrast and supporting keyboard navigation, make a big difference.

Why should we teach these ideas to school students? Because they are the developers of the future. When students build even a small app, we can ask them: Who might be excluded? What data do we really need? Could this be misused? These questions encourage them to see technology as something that serves people, not just something that works.

For next week, I'd like you to analyse a popular app and identify one ethical issue related to bias, privacy or accessibility, with a recommendation for improvement.

1a1udru.t: With the HSC approaching, many students are under pressure. Joining me is school counsellor Mark Davies. Mark, what are you seeing in schools?

We're seeing high levels of stress, particularly in Year 12. Some stress is normal and can be motivating, but for some students it becomes overwhelming. They stop sleeping well, withdraw from friends or feel that their entire future depends on one mark.

A huge one. Teachers see students every day, so they often notice changes before anyone else. A student who suddenly stops handing in work or seems withdrawn may be struggling. A simple, private check-in, like 'I've noticed you seem tired lately; how are you going?', can make a real difference.
Should teachers try to solve the problem themselves?

No. Teachers aren't counsellors, and they shouldn't try to be. Their role is to notice, listen and refer students to the wellbeing team. Every school has procedures for this, and teachers should follow them, especially if there's any concern about a student's safety.

Clear assessment schedules help a lot, so students aren't hit with several tasks in the same week. Teachers can also teach study skills, like breaking revision into small steps. And it's important that we talk about pathways. Students need to hear that there are many routes to university and careers, including alternative entry schemes and TAFE.
Keep communication open, encourage balance, like exercise, sleep and time with friends, and avoid adding pressure about marks. Remind them that you're proud of their effort.

ffklvs.t:
Good morning, colleagues. I want to talk about assessment, but not the kind that ends with a mark in a report. I'm talking about assessment for learning: the everyday practices that tell us, during a lesson, what students understand and what we should do next.

Research over several decades has shown that formative assessment, when done well, is one of the most powerful ways to improve student achievement. The key idea is simple. Teaching is only effective if we know whether students have learned what we intended. If we wait until the end-of-topic test, it's often too late to help.

So what does good formative assessment look like in a maths classroom? First, clear learning intentions. Students should know what they are learning and what success looks like. For example, "I can solve two-step equations and check my answer by substitution."

Second, frequent checks for understanding. Mini whiteboards, hinge questions and exit tickets allow us to gather evidence from every student, not just the confident volunteers. A well-designed hinge question has wrong answers that reveal specific misconceptions. If many students choose the same wrong answer, we know exactly what to reteach.

Third, feedback that moves learning forward. A mark alone tells a student very little. Comments such as "Check the sign when you move a term across the equals sign" are far more useful. Even better, give students time in class to act on the feedback.

Finally, involve students in assessing their own work and each other's. When students mark worked solutions against clear criteria, they begin to understand what quality looks like and become more independent learners.

None of this requires more marking. In fact, it often requires less, because we focus our effort where it makes a difference. I'd encourage each of you to choose one strategy to try in your classes this term.

5tpgxj.t: Good morning, everyone. A quick message about parking. From Monday, the staff car park near the gym will be closed for resurfacing for about two weeks. Please use the overflow car park behind the library instead. If that's full, you're allowed to park in the church car park on Smith Street, but only before eight-fifteen. Thanks for your patience.

5v2r8c.t: Have you started planning the Year 7 fractions unit yet?
I've had a look at last year's program, but honestly, I think it needs changing. The results were really disappointing.
I noticed that too. Most kids could follow the steps, but they didn't understand what a fraction actually is.
Exactly. So I was thinking we should start with a week of hands-on work. Fraction walls, paper folding, maybe measuring with rulers.
Good idea. But we've only got six weeks, and the common test is in week seven.
I know. Maybe we cut the worksheet revision lesson at the end and use online quizzes for homework instead.
That could work. Let's meet on Thursday after school and draft it properly.

1x55kuk.t:
Good afternoon, and congratulations on your first teaching positions. I've been in schools for twenty-six years, and I want to share three pieces of advice that I wish someone had given me.

First, don't try to be perfect. In your first year, you will plan lessons that don't work, you'll mark tasks too slowly and you'll forget at least one duty. That's normal. What matters is that you reflect, ask for help and improve. The teachers who struggle most are often the ones who hide their problems because they think everyone else is coping.

Second, relationships come before content. Students will not care how much mathematics you know until they know that you care about them. Learn names in the first week, notice when someone is absent and greet your classes at the door. These small things build trust, and trust makes classroom management much easier.

Third, protect your energy. Teaching is a marathon, not a sprint. Set yourself a finishing time each evening and keep at least one day of the weekend free. Use the resources your faculty already has instead of creating everything yourself. And please, eat lunch. I've seen too many new teachers spend every break on the photocopier.

Finally, remember why you chose this profession. On difficult days, think of the student whose face lit up when they finally understood something. Those moments are the reason we do this job. Thank you.

1r7pirj.t: Attention all staff. Due to scheduled maintenance, the school Wi-Fi network will be unavailable this Thursday from twelve o'clock until approximately two-thirty. Wired computers in the library and the computer labs will not be affected. If you were planning an online lesson during that time, please download any materials you need beforehand. We apologise for the inconvenience.

6ruit0.t: Thanks for seeing me. I'd like to buy some robotics kits for the Year 9 IPT class.
Sure. How many are you thinking of, and what's the cost?
Ideally ten kits, so students can work in groups of three. They're about two hundred and fifty dollars each.
So two and a half thousand. That's more than the faculty has left this year.
I know. But the kits are reusable for years, and they'd also be used by the coding club.
Could you start with five this year and buy the rest next year?
That might work if students work in groups of six for now. It's not ideal, but it's better than nothing.
Okay. Send me a written quote and I'll approve five.

53qxq7.t: Today I'm joined by Dr Priya Nair, who researches data privacy in schools. Dr Nair, why should parents be concerned?

Well, schools today collect an enormous amount of information: attendance, grades, behaviour notes, medical details and, increasingly, data from learning apps. Much of that is stored by private companies, and in the last few years there have been several breaches in which student information was exposed.
What kind of harm can that cause?

In the worst cases, identity theft, because children's records are valuable to criminals. Their identities often aren't checked for years, so fraud can go unnoticed for a long time. But there's also a quieter risk: information about a student's behaviour or learning difficulties could follow them in ways that are unfair.
So what should schools be doing?

Three things. First, collect only what they actually need. Second, check carefully where data is stored and who can access it before they adopt a new app. And third, teach students about privacy, so they understand that 'free' apps are often paid for with their data.

Teachers play a big role. They should never send student information through personal email or messaging apps, and they should think twice before signing their class up to a new website, however useful it seems.

16gzacv.t: Hi Sarah, it's Mark from student services. Just letting you know that the school counsellor will be at our school on Mondays and Wednesdays this term, not Tuesdays as before. Could you please tell your Year Nine students? Also, if any students need an urgent appointment on other days, they can come to the front office and we'll arrange a phone call with the counsellor. Thanks.

ya9f9s.t: Hassan, have you got a minute? You seemed a bit distracted today.
Sorry, Miss. I'm just really tired.
Is everything okay? You've missed the last two homework tasks as well.
I've been working more shifts at the restaurant. My dad's been sick, so I'm helping out with money.
That sounds really hard. Thank you for telling me. How many hours are you working?
About twenty a week now, mostly at night.
That's a lot on top of Year 11. Would you be okay if I spoke to your year adviser? We might be able to give you some extensions and help you plan your study time.
Yeah, that would help. I don't want to fall behind.

kmm473.t:
Today I want to talk about resilience, which we can define as the ability to adapt and recover when things go wrong. It's a word you'll hear a lot in schools, and sometimes it's misunderstood.

Resilience doesn't mean never feeling upset, and it certainly doesn't mean telling students to 'toughen up'. Resilient people still experience stress and disappointment. The difference is that they have strategies and support that help them recover.

Research suggests three things matter most. The first is relationships. Young people who have at least one caring adult in their lives, whether a parent, a coach or a teacher, cope much better with difficulties. The second is a sense of competence: the belief that effort can lead to improvement. This is where classroom practice really matters. When teachers praise strategies and persistence rather than intelligence, students learn that setbacks are part of learning. The third is practical skills, such as breaking problems into smaller steps, asking for help and managing stress through sleep, exercise and time with friends.

For teachers, the message is encouraging. You don't need to run a special program to build resilience. Every time you help a student try again after a poor test result, or show them how to tackle a difficult problem one step at a time, you are teaching resilience. In mathematics, in particular, students face problems they cannot immediately solve, which makes your classroom an ideal place to practise it.

nhfzpi.t: Good morning, Year Eleven. This is a reminder that your Mathematics Advanced assessment task is due next Friday, the fourteenth, by three o'clock. It must be submitted online through the learning platform, not by email. If you are ill on the due date, you must submit an illness and misadventure form with a medical certificate within three school days.

18u8mo2.t: So, for question five, I gave this student three out of four. What did you give?
I gave two. They set up the equation correctly, but they made an error solving it.
Yes, but the guidelines say you can still award the method mark if the working is clear after an error.
Let me look again... You're right. The method's fine from that point on. Three it is.
What about question eight? I think we're both being too generous there.
Agreed. Most students just wrote the answer without any explanation. Let's take it down to one mark for those.
Okay. We'll need to tell Sophie and James so they can adjust their classes too.

1o9oo7z.t:
Hi everyone. Two years ago I was sitting exactly where you are, so I want to share what worked for me and what I wish I'd done differently.

The biggest mistake I made in Term 1 was thinking the HSC was a long way off. I did my homework, but I didn't really revise. By Term 3, I had a mountain of topics I'd half forgotten. So my first piece of advice is to review a little every week from now. Even thirty minutes on old topics makes a huge difference.

Second, past papers. I started doing them in August, but I should have started earlier, topic by topic. And don't just check whether you got the right answer. Read the marking guidelines and the markers' comments. That's where I learned how to set out my working so I didn't lose easy marks.

Third, look after your health. In the trial exams, I barely slept, and I did worse than I expected. For the actual HSC, I kept a routine: study in the morning, exercise in the afternoon and no screens after ten. I felt so much calmer.

And finally, ask for help. Teachers really do want to help you, and many of them run extra sessions. I went to the maths revision sessions every Thursday, and that's where things finally clicked for me. Good luck, everyone. You can do this.

fe6x9y.t: This is a message from the front office. The lost property box is full again. It contains more than forty jumpers, twenty water bottles and several calculators. Any items not collected by the end of next week will be donated to charity. If your name is written on an item, we will return it to you. Please check the box outside the office at recess or lunch.

4cm7j2.t: So, Harmony Day is three weeks away. Where are we up to?
Well, we've got eight cultural groups who want to run food stalls, and the dance group is preparing a performance.
Great. What about the maths faculty? Last year we did nothing.
I had an idea: we could run a maths around the world activity. Different counting systems, patterns in Islamic art, that kind of thing.
I love that. Could students from Year 8 help run it?
Yes, I'll ask my class tomorrow. We just need a room and some printing money.
I'll book the library and ask the deputy about the budget.

1uybw97.t:
Thank you all for coming. In our school, more than seventy percent of students speak a language other than English at home, so building strong partnerships with families is something we have to do deliberately.

I'd like to start with a story. A few years ago, a teacher here was worried because a Year Seven boy never handed in homework. She sent three emails home and got no reply, so she assumed his parents didn't care. When she finally phoned with an interpreter, she discovered that his mother couldn't read English, and his father worked night shifts. They were extremely concerned about their son and very grateful for the call.

The lesson is that silence doesn't mean a lack of interest. Families may face language barriers, unfamiliar school systems or long working hours. Some come from cultures where questioning teachers is considered disrespectful, so they won't contact us even when they are worried.

So what can we do? First, use phone calls and interpreters, not just emails and newsletters. Second, make the first contact positive. Call home to share good news before you ever need to discuss a problem. Third, explain how our system works: things like assessment schedules, reports and subject selection can be confusing for families who were educated overseas.

When families feel welcome and informed, they become our strongest partners in their children's learning.

x6sjvp.t: Hello, this is Anna from learning support. I'm calling about Mia in your Year Eight maths class. Her new learning plan has been finalised, and it includes extra time in tests and access to a reader for worded problems. I'll email you a copy today. Could you please let me know by Thursday which upcoming assessments she'll need these adjustments for?

g5chxc.t: Are you in favour of the plan to stream Year 7 maths classes by ability next year?
Partly. It makes planning easier, and the top students would be challenged more.
True, but I worry about the bottom class. Research says students in lower streams often fall further behind.
That's a fair point. And once students are in a low group, it's hard for them to move up.
Maybe we could keep mixed classes in Year 7 and only stream from Year 9.
That might work. Or we could have flexible groups within each class, so students can move depending on the topic.
Let's suggest both options at the faculty meeting.

1ekt8iv.t: Dr Chen, how common is ADHD among secondary students?
Estimates vary, but roughly five percent of children and adolescents have ADHD. So in an average school, most teachers will have one or more students with ADHD in their classes every year.
What does it look like in the classroom?

It's often misunderstood. People imagine a boy running around the room, but many students, especially girls, have the inattentive type. They may seem daydreamy, lose track of instructions or leave work unfinished. They're sometimes labelled lazy, which is very damaging.
What practical strategies can teachers use?

Some of the most effective are also the simplest. Break tasks into smaller steps with clear checkpoints. Give instructions both verbally and in writing. Seat the student where distractions are minimal, and allow short movement breaks. In maths, for example, a student might complete five questions, show the teacher, then do the next five, instead of facing a whole page at once.
And how important is the relationship with the teacher?

Extremely. Students with ADHD often receive far more negative feedback than their peers. A teacher who notices their strengths and gives specific praise can make a huge difference to their motivation and self-esteem.

d53t67.t: Hi Year Ten, it's Ms Patel, the careers adviser. A reminder that work experience forms are due this Friday. You need signatures from your employer, your parent or carer, and your year adviser. Students who haven't found a placement yet should come and see me in the careers office at lunchtime on Wednesday, and I'll help you contact some local businesses.

8t6b4f.t: Sir, I'm trying to decide between Maths Standard and Maths Advanced for Year 11.
What are you thinking of doing after school?
Maybe engineering, but I'm not sure yet.
Then I'd strongly recommend Advanced. Most engineering degrees assume you've done at least Advanced, and some recommend Extension 1.
But my friends say Standard is easier and gives a better ATAR.
It might feel easier, but the scaling usually favours Advanced. And if you drop to Standard, it's much harder to go back up later.
Okay. What if I find Advanced too hard?
Then we'd talk about it early in Term 1. And you can always come to the Thursday help sessions.

1fonb3v.t:
Thank you for inviting me. I'm a software engineer, and I work for a company that builds apps for hospitals. When I was at school, I had no idea this job existed. I liked maths, but I thought computing was something boys did after school playing games.

What changed my mind was a holiday program in Year Ten. For one week, we worked in teams to design an app that helped elderly people remember their medication. I realised that technology could solve real problems for real people, and that it needed creativity and teamwork as much as coding.

Today, women still make up less than a third of the technology workforce in Australia. That's not because girls aren't capable. In fact, girls often do very well in mathematics and computing at school. The problem is that many never imagine themselves in these roles, partly because they don't see people like them doing the work.

So I have two messages tonight. To students: if you enjoy solving problems, technology could be for you, whatever you look like and whatever your background. Try a coding club, enter a competition, or ask about a holiday program. To parents and teachers: encourage girls to keep studying mathematics, even if they're not sure about their future. Mathematics keeps doors open. I nearly closed that door myself, and I'm so glad someone encouraged me to keep it open.

1cj45mv.t: This Friday, our school will take part in Clean Up Australia Day. Each roll call class will be given gloves and bags and assigned an area of the school or the local park. Please wear sensible shoes and bring a hat and a water bottle. The class that collects the most rubbish will win a pizza lunch, so let's make our school and neighbourhood shine.

1mnhefx.t: So the quote for solar panels on the hall roof came in yesterday.
About sixty thousand dollars, but there's a government grant that would cover half.
That's still thirty thousand from our budget. How long until it pays for itself?
The installer estimates around six years, based on our current electricity use.
That seems reasonable. And the panels last at least twenty years, don't they?
Yes. Plus, the IPT classes could use the live data from the system for projects.
Good point. Let's put it on the agenda for the next P&C meeting.

1yadeja.t:
Good morning. I want to show you how sustainability can become one of the most engaging contexts for teaching statistics.

Three years ago, my Year Ten students were bored by textbook data about fictional shoe sizes. So we started using real environmental data instead. The Bureau of Meteorology publishes temperature and rainfall records for every region of Australia, going back more than a hundred years. Students choose a location that matters to them, perhaps where they grew up, or where their grandparents live, and investigate how the climate has changed.

The mathematics is genuine. Students calculate means and medians for different decades, draw box plots, identify outliers and discuss whether changes are significant or just natural variation. Some go further and use spreadsheets to create trend lines.

What surprised me most was the quality of discussion. Students debated how to choose fair comparison periods and whether a few extreme years could distort the results. They were thinking like statisticians.

Of course, there are challenges. Real data is messy. There are missing values and changes in measuring equipment, so students need guidance. Some topics, like climate change, can also cause anxiety, so it's important to focus on investigation and solutions rather than fear.

But overall, I've found that when data is real and personally meaningful, students engage far more deeply than with any textbook example.

t3nydk.t: Hi everyone. Just a reminder that Monday is a staff development day, so there are no students on site. We'll start at eight-thirty in the library with a session on supporting students with anxiety. After morning tea, faculties will meet to work on next year's programs. Lunch will be provided. Please bring your laptop and charger.

ea650.t: Thanks for letting me observe your Year 8 lesson. How do you think it went?
I think the explanation was clear, but the class got noisy during the group task.
I agree. Your explanation of ratios was excellent, and the real-life examples worked well. The group task was a good idea too.
The instructions were only verbal, and some groups weren't sure what to do, so they started chatting.
That makes sense. Should I put them on the board next time?
Yes, and give each student a role. Try it with the same class next week, and I'll come back to see how it goes.

v29k2q.t:
Today's topic is reflective practice, which simply means thinking carefully about your own teaching in order to improve it. Every experienced teacher you admire does this, often without even noticing.

Reflection isn't the same as worrying. Lying awake replaying a lesson that went badly is not reflection. Reflection is structured. It asks specific questions: What did I want students to learn? What evidence do I have that they learned it? What will I do differently next time?

The key word there is evidence. Too often, we judge a lesson by how it felt. A lively, noisy lesson might feel successful, but did students actually learn the content? On the other hand, a quiet lesson might feel flat, yet students may have made real progress. Exit tickets, student work and short quizzes give you evidence beyond your feelings.

There are many ways to make reflection a habit. Some teachers keep a brief journal, writing three sentences after each lesson. Others record a lesson occasionally and watch it back, which can be uncomfortable but very revealing. Many find it most useful to reflect with a colleague, because another person notices things we miss.

During your placements, you've been required to write reflections. I encourage you not to see them as paperwork, but as the beginning of a professional habit that will make you a better teacher throughout your career.

tvxvqu.t: Attention all staff and students. Some of you have received an email that appears to come from the school, asking you to reset your password using a link. This email is not from us. Please do not click the link. Delete the email, and if you have already entered your password, change it immediately and contact the IT help desk on extension two-four-five.

przprp.t: Thank you for coming in, Mrs Ali. I understand Zara has been upset about some messages.
Yes. A group of girls created a chat and they've been posting photos of her with nasty comments.
I'm very sorry. Has Zara kept copies of the messages?
She took screenshots. Here they are.
Thank you, that's really helpful. I'll speak to the students involved today, and their parents will be contacted.
Will Zara be in trouble for telling?
Not at all. She did exactly the right thing. We'll also check in with her every day this week, and the counsellor can see her if she'd like.

r40tfe.t: With me is Professor Tom Walsh, who studies young people and technology. Professor, is social media harming teenagers?

It's more complicated than a simple yes or no. For many young people, social media is where they maintain friendships, find communities and explore interests. For teenagers from minority groups or rural areas, these connections can be really valuable.
But there are concerns about mental health.

Yes, and they're real. Heavy use, especially late at night, is linked to poorer sleep, and poor sleep affects mood. Some platforms are designed to keep users scrolling, and constant comparison with carefully edited images can affect self-esteem, particularly among girls.
Some governments are introducing age limits. Do you support that?

I understand the motivation, but age limits are difficult to enforce. Many children simply lie about their age. I think the bigger priorities are safer design, such as limits on endless scrolling, and education, so that young people understand how platforms work.

Schools can teach digital literacy across subjects, involve parents and, importantly, listen to students. Young people often have very good ideas about what would make their online lives healthier, but they're rarely asked.

oumtd2.t: Good morning, staff and students. Please note that today's Year 9 assembly has been moved from the quadrangle to the school hall because of the rain. It will now start at 9:15 instead of 9:00, so roll call will run for an extra fifteen minutes. Year 9 teachers, please bring your class rolls to the hall. Thank you.

ixv8c.t: Hi, it's Sam from the maths faculty. I won't be in tomorrow, I've got a medical appointment. Could you organise a casual for my classes?
Of course. Have you left work for them?
Yes, it's all in the blue folder on my desk. Periods one, two and four. Period three is free.
Great. I'll book Mrs Lee. She's taught maths before.

1luzs36.t: Just a reminder about the Year 11 exam next week. Students may use their own approved calculator, but it must not be a graphics calculator for the Standard course. If a student forgets their calculator, there are ten spares in the faculty office.

You must wear closed-toe shoes, because it's an industrial site, and you won't be allowed to take photos inside for security reasons. Bring a notebook, because you'll need notes for your assessment task.

1scneoq.t: Have you seen the elective numbers for next year?
Yes, IPT's down to eighteen students. Last year we had thirty.
That's a big drop. Why do you think that is?
I think the new software engineering course is attracting a lot of them. And we didn't really promote IPT at subject selection night.
Maybe we should run a taster lesson for Year 10 next term.

1cck6x8.t: Hi Mark, it's Sam in room B12. The projector in my room keeps switching off after about ten minutes, and then it takes five minutes to turn back on. I think it might be overheating, because the fan is very noisy. I've got Year 8 there all day tomorrow, so if you could have a look before 9 am, that would be great. Thanks.

17225jc.t: Today you'll work in groups of four to design a budget for a class party. Each person has a role. The leader keeps the group on track. The recorder writes down your decisions. The calculator checks all the maths, and the presenter will explain your budget to the class at the end. You have a maximum of two hundred dollars, and you must include food, drinks and decorations.

1b239ct.t: As the trial exams get closer, I want to share three tips. First, study in short blocks of about forty-five minutes, with a short break in between. Second, practise past papers under timed conditions, not just your notes. And third, look after yourselves: sleep at least eight hours, and don't give up exercise completely. Remember, the counsellor is available every day at lunch if you're feeling stressed.

gmvit2.t: How did you find your first term?
Honestly, exhausting. The planning takes me hours every night.
That's very normal. Are you using the faculty's shared units?
Not really, I've been making everything from scratch.
Don't. Use the shared programs and adapt them. Spend your energy on getting to know the students instead.

19ku3ar.t: Do you like games, robots or apps? Then come along to the new junior coding club, starting next Wednesday in Lab C4 at lunchtime. It's open to Years 7 to 9, and no experience is needed. We'll start with Scratch and move on to programming robots later in the term. Places are limited to twenty-five, so sign up with Mr Ahmed by Monday.

bhg4ul.t: My daughter says she'll never use algebra in real life.
That's a common view! Actually, she uses maths whenever she cooks with you. Doubling a recipe is proportional reasoning.
Really? I hadn't thought of that.
Yes, and if she wants to be a nurse, as she mentioned, she'll calculate medication doses using formulas every day.

1xhv4h4.t: This afternoon at 2:10 we'll hold a lockdown drill. When you hear the continuous siren, lock your classroom door, close the blinds, turn off the lights and keep students away from windows and doors. Students must stay silent. Mark the roll and wait for the all-clear announcement. Please do not open the door to anyone during the drill, even if they say they're a staff member.

2msgy8.t: Before we finish, a quick reminder: all Year 10 assessment marks must be entered into Sentral by Friday the 21st. Please also upload two marked samples, one high and one middle, to the faculty drive for moderation. If you're running late for any reason, let me know by Wednesday so I can tell the deputy. Reports go to parents the following week.

1w98jka.t: New staff laptops will be distributed in the library next Tuesday between 3:15 and 5 pm. Please bring your old laptop and charger, as these must be returned at the same time. Make sure you have backed up all your files to OneDrive beforehand, because old devices will be wiped. Staff who can't attend should contact the IT office to arrange another time.

I can do the first hour, but I have to leave at 6:30 to pick up my son.
No problem. Maria can take over from 6:30 to 7:30.
And who's talking to parents about senior courses?
I will. I've printed fifty copies of the course guide.

4zlagw.t: As you know, under the NSW policy, students must keep their phones switched off and out of sight for the whole school day, including recess and lunch. If a student uses their phone, it will be held at the front office until the end of the day. If you need to contact your child urgently, please call the front office, and we'll pass on the message immediately.

16oda9z.t: Sir, what's in the test on Thursday?
Everything from the measurement unit: perimeter, area and volume. Not surface area, though. We'll do that next term.
Can we use a formula sheet?
Yes, I'll give you one in the test. But you still need to know how to use the formulas.
Okay. Will there be worded problems?
Yes, about a third of the marks.

1t8ikv8.t: When you write report comments, start with a genuine strength, then give one or two specific areas for improvement, and finish with advice the student can actually act on. Avoid vague comments like 'try harder'. And always proofread carefully: parents notice spelling mistakes, and a comment with another student's name in it looks terrible.

1dd3col.t: For Friday's athletics carnival, every teacher has a duty. You'll find your role on the roster in the staffroom. The buses leave at 8:30, and staff must be at the stadium by 8:45 to set up. Please bring a hat, sunscreen and plenty of water. If it rains heavily, we'll postpone, and I'll send a message by 7 am.

17thify.t: We're moving all classes to the new learning platform from Term 3. To help you, there are three training sessions: Monday after school, Wednesday at lunchtime, and an online session on Thursday evening. Each one takes about an hour, and they all cover the same content, so you only need to attend one. Please register through the staff portal.

fduxcy.t: One of the simplest strategies I use is mini whiteboards. I ask a question, everyone writes the answer, and on my signal, they hold the boards up. In five seconds I can see who understands and who doesn't. The key is to keep it quick, and never embarrass students who get it wrong. Instead, I note who needs help and work with them while the others continue.

1t0f6bt.t: Hello, this is Dr Lee from Western Sydney University. I'm very sorry, but I can no longer visit your school on Wednesday for Maths Week, because I've been asked to attend a conference interstate. I could come the following Monday instead, at the same time, if that suits. Please call me back on 9685 2200. Again, my apologies.

17x63dk.t: I'm a bit worried about Omar in my Year 10 class. He's been really quiet and he hasn't handed in any work for two weeks.
Thanks for telling me. Has he said anything?
No, but he looks tired and he's been late a lot.
I'll call his family today and organise a meeting with the counsellor. Could you put your notes in the wellbeing system?
Yes, I'll do that this afternoon.

i2xmq1.t: I want to be very clear about the IPT project. If any part of your code or report is copied from another student or from the internet without acknowledgement, including AI-generated code, you will receive zero for that section. You may use online resources to learn, but you must reference them. If you're unsure, ask your teacher before submitting.

9arjwp.t: I need to collect evidence for my proficient accreditation. Where do I start?
Start with the standards. For each one, choose an example from your teaching, like a lesson plan or student work.
How many pieces of evidence do I need?
Usually around five sets, annotated to show which standards they meet. And your principal has to sign off at the end.
Okay, I'll start with my Year 8 unit.

yffawy.t: Our budget for next year is eight thousand dollars, which is less than this year. The biggest expense will be replacing old textbooks for Year 9, about three thousand dollars. I'd also like to spend one thousand on professional learning. That leaves four thousand for resources like calculators and puzzles. If you have suggestions, please email me before the end of term.

tek00b.t: Miss, I couldn't finish my assignment. My grandmother was in hospital last week.
I'm sorry to hear that. Is she okay now?
Good. You'll need to fill in the illness and misadventure form, and get a note from your parents. Then I can give you an extension until next Wednesday.

lqieu7.t: Here's an activity my Year 9s love. Each pair rolls two dice fifty times and records the totals. Then we combine the class data on a spreadsheet. Students are always surprised that seven comes up most often. It leads to a great discussion about why: there are six ways to make seven, but only one way to make two or twelve.
